prompt: Do you think that this income statement is based on IFRS? Justify with one element.
modelAnswer: No (at least not fully IFRS-compliant). It shows an 'extraordinary result' line – IAS 1.87 prohibits presenting any item of income or expense as extraordinary. (Any one justified element suffices.)
keyPoints: Extraordinary items are prohibited under IFRS (IAS 1.87)

steps.title: Scan for elements IFRS does not allow
steps.why: IAS 1.87: no item of income or expense may be presented as 'extraordinary' – neither in the income statement nor in the notes.
steps.result: No – not an IFRS income statement

pitfalls: Arguing with 'by nature' – presenting by nature IS allowed under IFRS, so it is no evidence.

prompt: Do you think that this income statement is a consolidated income statement? Justify with one element.
modelAnswer: Probably not. A consolidated income statement would split net income between owners of the parent and non-controlling interests, and would typically show a share of profit of associates; neither appears. (Hint for a consolidated statement would be the opposite elements.)
keyPoints: No split of net income into group share / non-controlling interests
No share of profit of associates

steps.title: Recall what a consolidated income statement must show
steps.why: IFRS 10/IAS 1: net income is split into 'attributable to owners of the parent' and 'attributable to non-controlling interests'; associates appear as 'share of profit of associates'.

steps.title: Check the statement
lines: No split of the net result into group share / NCI
No share of profit of associates
steps.result: Probably not consolidated – an individual income statement

prompt: How is it possible to have 'rent and associated charges' although the company applies IFRS 16 to its leases?
modelAnswer: IFRS 16 offers two optional exemptions for lessees: short-term leases (lease term of 12 months or less) and leases of low-value assets (≈ USD 5,000 when new); their payments are expensed straight-line. In addition, 'associated charges' include non-lease (service) components such as maintenance, cleaning or service charges, and variable payments not included in the lease liability – these are expensed. All other leases appear as right-of-use assets (hence the depreciation line).
keyPoints: Service/non-lease components and variable payments are expensed

steps.title: Recall the IFRS 16 lessee model
steps.why: In principle every lease → right-of-use asset + lease liability, expenses = depreciation (the line 'depreciation of right-of-use assets') + interest. So a rent expense needs a reason.

steps.title: Reason 1 – optional exemptions
lines: Leases of low-value assets (≈ USD 5,000 when new, e.g. laptops)
steps.why: For these the lessee may expense the payments straight-line as rent.

steps.title: Reason 2 – payments outside the lease liability
steps.why: Service components (maintenance, cleaning, service charges = 'associated charges') and variable payments not linked to an index are not part of the lease liability and are expensed.

prompt: Explain why there is no goodwill amortisation in 2022.
modelAnswer: Under IFRS goodwill has an indefinite useful life and is not amortised (IFRS 3/IAS 38); instead it is tested for impairment at least annually (IAS 36). As no impairment was necessary, the amount is unchanged.
keyPoints: Goodwill is not amortised under IFRS

steps.title: Recall the IFRS rule
steps.why: Goodwill has an indefinite useful life → it is NOT amortised (IFRS 3). Instead IAS 36 requires an impairment test at least once a year.

steps.title: Apply to the note
steps.why: The test did not show an impairment, so goodwill stays at 365 M£.
steps.result: No amortisation; annual impairment test → no loss in 2022

prompt: Explain briefly how the recoverable amount of goodwill is calculated in general, and for this airline in particular.
modelAnswer: Goodwill does not generate cash flows on its own, so it is allocated to the cash-generating unit(s) that benefit from it and tested at that level. The recoverable amount of the CGU is the higher of its fair value less costs of disposal and its value in use (present value of future cash flows). If the CGU's carrying amount (incl. goodwill) exceeds it, the impairment loss reduces goodwill first. Here: the airline CGU's recoverable amount is its value in use – cash flows of the five-year plan, extrapolated at 2% long-term growth, discounted at a pre-tax rate (11.0% in 2022).
keyPoints: Recoverable amount = higher of FV less costs of disposal and value in use
Value in use = PV of future cash flows
Airline: 5-year plan, 2% growth, pre-tax discount rate

steps.title: Test level: CGU
steps.why: Goodwill generates no cash flows on its own, so it is allocated to the cash-generating unit(s) that benefit from the acquisition and tested together with their assets.

steps.title: General formula
lines: Recoverable amount = HIGHER of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use
Value in use = present value of the CGU's expected future cash flows
Impairment if carrying amount (incl. goodwill) > recoverable amount → goodwill reduced first

steps.title: This airline
lines: Recoverable amount = value in use of the airline CGU
Cash flows from the board-approved 5-year plan
Discounted with a pre-tax rate (11.0% in 2022)
steps.result: VIU-based test at CGU level, 5-year plan + 2% growth, 11% pre-tax rate

prompt: How do the changes in the discount rate and the fuel price assumption affect the recoverable amount? Are the 2022 assumptions stricter (more prudent) than in 2021?
modelAnswer: A higher discount rate (9.5% → 11.0%) reduces the present value of future cash flows. A higher fuel price assumption ($650 → $900/t) increases expected costs and reduces forecast cash flows. Both changes lower the value in use and therefore the recoverable amount, i.e. the headroom over the carrying amount shrinks and an impairment becomes more likely. So the 2022 assumptions are stricter / more prudent than those of 2021.
keyPoints: Higher discount rate → lower present value
Higher fuel price → lower cash flows

steps.title: Effect of the discount rate (9.5% → 11.0%)
steps.why: A higher discount rate lowers the present value of the same future cash flows → value in use falls.

steps.title: Effect of the fuel price ($650 → $900 per tonne)
steps.why: Fuel is a major cost: higher price → lower forecast cash flows → value in use falls.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.why: Both changes reduce the recoverable amount and the headroom over the carrying amount; an impairment becomes more likely.
steps.result: 2022 assumptions are stricter / more prudent than 2021

pitfalls: Concluding that a lower recoverable amount means an impairment was booked – it only reduces the headroom (goodwill was unchanged).

prompt: Outline the reasoning for each period and present the accounting impacts for N1 to N4.
modelAnswer:
Depreciation 300,000/10 = 30,000 per year.
N1: no indication of impairment (production as planned) → no test required for PPE; depreciation 30,000; carrying amount 270,000.
N2: still no indication → depreciation 30,000; carrying amount 240,000.
N3: the new law is an external indication → test. Carrying amount before test 210,000; recoverable amount = higher of FV less costs to sell (170,000 − 18,000 = 152,000) and value in use (175,000) = 175,000 → impairment loss 35,000 (expense); carrying amount 175,000.
N4: depreciation on the new basis 175,000 / 7 remaining years = 25,000 → 150,000. The transition measure indicates that the impairment may have reversed → recoverable amount = max(200,000 − 15,000; 190,000) = 190,000. The reversal is capped at the carrying amount without impairment: 300,000 − 4 × 30,000 = 180,000 → reversal 30,000 (income); carrying amount 180,000 (then depreciation 30,000 per year again).

steps.title: N1 and N2 – no indication of impairment
steps.why: IAS 36: PP&E is only tested when there is an INDICATION of impairment. Production runs as planned → no test, even though value in use is slightly below the carrying amount.

steps.title: N3 – new law = external indication → impairment test
N4 – new depreciation basis
steps.why: After an impairment, the new carrying amount is depreciated over the remaining useful life (7 years).

steps.title: N4 – transition measure = indication of reversal
lines: Cap: carrying amount had there been no impairment = 300,000 − 4 × 30,000 = 180,000
steps.result: Carrying amount end N4: 180,000 (afterwards depreciation 30,000 p.a. again)

pitfalls: Testing in N1/N2 without an indication.
Reversing up to the recoverable amount (190,000) instead of the cap (180,000).
